title: Is our Foundation Years programme on track?
intro: Ten statements, about five minutes. Answer for your school on an ordinary day. This is a reflection tool to start a conversation. It is not an assessment of your school. Your answers stay in your browser and are not sent anywhere.

areas.label: Relationships
areas.advice: Strengthening relationships often starts with routines at arrival, transitions and moments of need. A short walk-through of the school day, looking at the child, usually shows where to begin.

areas.label: Play
areas.advice: Protect long, uninterrupted play and watch it before stepping in. Teachers who learn what to look for in play tend to see much more of what children can do.

areas.label: Language
areas.advice: Pausing, waiting and using children's home language give every child more room to speak. Small changes in how adults ask questions can make a large difference.

areas.label: Thinking
areas.advice: Asking children to explain how they worked something out, and treating second tries as normal, makes thinking visible. Thinking routines are a practical place to start.

areas.label: Seeing and planning
areas.advice: Write down a little of what you see, often, and use it to plan the next experience. Leaders who regularly look at what children experience, not only at documents, get a truer picture.

questions.text: When a child arrives, an adult greets them by name and notices how they seem to be feeling.
Children know which adult to go to when they need help, and they do.
Children have long stretches of uninterrupted time to choose and play.
Adults watch play for a while before stepping in or directing it.
Adults pause and wait for children's answers before moving on.
Children can use their home language in school and it is welcomed.
Children are asked to explain or show how they worked something out.
A second try, or a mistake, is treated as a normal part of learning.
Teachers write down what they see children doing, and use it to plan what comes next.
School leaders regularly spend time in classrooms looking at what children experience, not only at documents.
